items.rss_description: Independent Agents - A Forward View Agent & Broker ITL Editorial Team Fri, 10/23/2026 - 13:36 Economic simulations now forecast fiscal health across 1,900 U.S. localities, helping agents anticipate consumer affordability shifts and community financial stress. October 23, 2026 Image Local agents swim in the waters around them, and while a rising tide lifts all boats, that sucking sound before a tsunami hits shore is a clear signal that locality risk is a constant. It's good to be lucky with a rising tide, but luck is not a strategy. Simulations of the world are a way to describe observed reality and anticipate change, and modeling the changing economic tides of every locality in America (call that a list with 1,900 locations) is a good way to both reflect on what has happened since COVID-19 and to help those agents see what's coming next. Modeling Communities Like We Model Weather We simulate weather daily to anticipate storm tracks and estimate damage. We simulate climate change with variation in sea level, flood plains, and riverbanks. We simulate fire spread, hail fall, straight-line wind… and so, too, we should simulate the local economies of 1,900 communities across America. In a consumer-driven economy, simulating how America spends is like watching a developing hurricane pattern off the shore – is it intensifying or waning, is it heading for land or staying off the coast, what amount of intrusion to interior geographies will a footprint create, and will there be additional risks set in motion as the dynamics unfold, including supply chain and demand patterns that may also be interrupted or surged? Affordability and Fiscal Health as Key Signals Just as a student loan may go unpaid if post-graduate incomes are low, the choices households and individuals make on debts to service and debts to default are mirrored at businesses, organizations, and local communities, cities, and municipalities. These local priorities of affordability affect decisions on risk transfer and affect premiums – agents sit amid it all. (See this article on a data source to predict financial health, going beyond the backward-looking credit reports that insurers use.) Affordability is a key signal, as is the fiscal health of a locality. When you combine these with the inflows and outflows of households and businesses, any agency can make a plan for the year or two ahead and set in motion a process for continually navigating their locales. Looking Backward: The Affordability Crisis People living in houses and driving cars work at businesses and spend money in their communities. Unsurprisingly, changes in the economies of those communities are both observable and predictable. That matters to local agents. Looking backward, hindsight is usually 20/20 – higher uninsured driver populations occurred where affordability was lowest. More UM/UIM claims drive insurance costs higher, and rates may go up even further. In an economic downswing, rising costs and flat to slow wage increases force more budget stress on consumers. Where job loss escalates stress, things twist up even faster. Not only do consumers decide not to be insured, but they also change other spending habits. More businesses fail when customers can no longer afford them. Collections of tax revenue suffer when high earners migrate away and when business activity slows or falters. Taxes suffer further when sales slump, and property values deteriorate. These can lead to cuts in community services, and spiral from there. Emerging Patterns: From Data Centers to Remote Work Independent agents, brokers of all sizes, carriers, wholesalers, specialty, excess, and MGA/MGUs all compete in these predictable localities. And predictions for consumers, businesses, and even the localities are proving their value in understanding and pricing risk. Some localities see changes that are from emerging patterns of life and risk, like hyperscale data centers. Other changes are more subtle, like a work-from-anywhere job landscape that allows high earners to live wherever they want. Or what happens when AI shifts work tasks in legacy workflows or creates new ways of working? Boomtowns to ghost towns and everything in between paint the map of America -- parcel-by-parcel, building-by-building, business-by-business, organization-by-organization, job-by-job, and so, too, insurance and risk management dynamics. Some things change very slowly, while others shift abruptly, but the profound effect of "work anywhere" from COVID may be the most significant overarching impact in our generation and the next. Anticipating Economic Consequences We anticipate sudden changes to life patterns in a variety of peril-driven scenarios – hurricane, tornado, fire, severe convective storm – as well as in environmental scenarios like sea level change, cyclical patterns like El Niño, and even major disruptions like power outages, transportation interruptions, and cyber interference. Anticipating economic consequences, especially shifts in contribution to cash flow in community capital assets and liabilities, is another risk in the underlying infrastructure where all the other risks interact. Thriving localities add services and amenities, which attract more growth. Dwindling localities lay off public workers and renegotiate long-term liabilities while trying to improve local revenues with more taxes and fees. Debt offerings and the ability to service debt obligations are then most comparable to Ernest Hemingway's famous line on personal bankruptcy – which happens "gradually, then suddenly." New Analytics for Local Planning Analytics now exist for consumers, businesses, and their communities across the 1,900 localities that make up the investable and insurable economies of America. This observability of a locality, its finances, its threats/opportunities, and its ability to service its debts and obligations is summed across the consumer and business mix of their constituents and forecast against those changing elements to portray current and future years' planning horizons. Local agents can take heed. Situations with imminent insolvency are expected to make certain choices, while growth-busting upside creates better problems. Adapting to Local Reality While agents can always relocate, they are more likely to need to adapt to their local reality. While premium forecasts and business mix are constantly used in distribution planning and customer appetite focus, the pace of change has accelerated inside of the existing process steps. Using a locality stress index along with existing forecasts and affordability measures will make agents smarter in their marketplaces and quicker to react to change. This means that in troubled areas, expect more business failures, lapses, and non-payment of premiums in a dwindling premium pattern, yet a rise in risk for fraud, theft, and malicious mischief, including a heavier threat of arson. This includes household stress, too, where skyrocketing base rates have pushed daily budgeting stress onto most households for car and homeowner insurance into an affordability squeeze where many drivers are underinsured, overcommitting to large deductibles, or going all the way to lapsing insurance entirely and becoming uninsured drivers. What does luck look like? A common quote from successful businesses – "It's better to be lucky, even if you're good." Never has that been more relevant than today, as changes in local luck have magnified in recent years. Some places have a deep downside – rising taxes, failing businesses, public service degradation, municipal financial stress, drops in quality of life generally, and the ensuing changes in household composition from thriving to just holding on. Some places have all sunshine -- growth in incomes, formation of new jobs, infrastructure improvements, and engaged public services. To live in an uninvestable locality is the hallmark of being unlucky. The endpoints are always locality-based. It is where people live, where businesses operate, and where municipal authorities administer. For an agent, the forward look in these markets is flat to down. Fewer businesses for fewer booming households means fewer insurable assets. Even if premiums rise and commissions float with them, the total insurance value opportunity won't be in a boom cycle. The larger concern is a doom cycle. Investors are aware of the general migration trend outlined in this recent Census article , whereby large metro areas are losing residents, while many smaller metro areas are growing. Details matter, and this is where data and analytics add critical value: High earners are migrating away from large metro areas in fiscally troubled states. They are migrating to small and mid-sized metro areas: Boise, Idaho; Frisco, Texas. High earners are responsible for the majority of personal and property taxes, new business formation, and capital investments. Scoring the 1,900 Localities Across the observed 1,900 cities, the municipalities, consumers, and businesses are scored based on their future fiscal viability and likelihood to default across a set of debts (everyday bills, credit cards, car loans, mortgages, business loans, pension commitments, municipal bonds, etc.). Ranked near the top of the list is St. George, Utah, with a short-term debt ratio of 0.31, which represents total liabilities divided by total assets. St. George is representative of 60 mostly mid-sized "under the radar" cities that have low legacy liabilities and sustainable budgets and are growing their populations with a healthy taxpayer base. This is where you can feel comfortable doing business for the long term. Lucky local agents! Then there are plenty of typical "middling" cities, with budgets that are not sustainable over the long term due to underfunded pension and benefits liabilities. Steady as she goes for the next few years. On the other side of the scale – consider a poster child for fiscal mismanagement to the extent it appears on a list titled Uninvestable Cities. These cities are laying off public sector workers today as they struggle with revenue shortfalls. Most of these cities meet the technical definition of insolvency. They appear to have accelerating financial deterioration over the next 24 months, resulting in a highly likely outright fiscal crisis. Envision trying to do business in a city where high earners (lowest risk, rational decision-makers) are leaving. The businesses are shuttering, as well. New business formation is almost non-existent. The city struggles to fund basic services, while raising taxes. The residual population has lower FICO scores. Crime, including costly fraud, rises. The Resilience of Independent Agents Every year another study predicts the demise of independent agents. They are getting too old; they can't scale to digital; they can't compete with changing technology… add in AI. Yet every year independent agents remain a dominant force in commercial insurance and have never failed to impress in personal lines. Watch how they adapt across 1,900 localities as a way to keep insuring America. ADDITIONAL THOUGHTS PARKING LOT What has changed is almost everything all at once. Blame it on remote work options, but look at how many high-earner households opt to relocate for better taxes, better weather, better schools, better anything. Blame it on migration, but the businesses and services they need will follow them, while the ones that used to serve them will feel the loss. Blame it on anything you like, but the undeniable facts are that no one relocates to a state; they move to a specific location. The imbalances from losing localities to gaining localities are seen in shifts in income, housing, business formations/failures, and municipal financial resilience. To assess health, a current approach ties to the capital markets where municipalities trade their debt. Using a locality lens, it is possible to observe the condition of consumers, businesses, and municipalities. With modern data and analytics, we can track changes over time. Did all three (consumer, business, municipality) improve, stay the same, or deteriorate in the last few years? What is the effect of these local changes, and how fast are changes now occurring? What is in store for the next couple of years? The US is in the early stages of an economic transformation, by locality, and that means insurance agents have both local threats and opportunities. Like Detroit filing Chapter 9 bankruptcy in 2013, it is conceivable that other major cities may follow suit. No city is immune to stress in changing local economies, and dozens of large municipalities have a reckoning coming. The tax base within these cities (high-earner consumers and meaningful business tax bases) is departing at rates never seen before. Marty Ellingsworth

No city is immune to stress in changing local economies, and dozens of large municipalities have a reckoning coming. The tax base within these cities (high-earner consumers and meaningful business tax bases) is departing at rates never seen before. Marty Ellingsworth

items.title: When an AI Calls, Who Should Answer?
items.original_title: When an AI Calls, Who Should Answer?
items.rss_title: When an AI Calls, Who Should Answer?
items.rss_description: When an AI Calls, Who Should Answer? AI & Machine Learning ITL Editorial Team Wed, 10/21/2026 - 13:19 Blocking Meta's AI agent on your website won't stop it from calling. Insurers need a plan to handle these calls. October 22, 2026 Image A consumer's AI agent can now call an insurer and ask for a quote. The possibility of such calls leaves carriers with two bad options: putting a licensed person on the line with a machine, or risk hanging up on a real person. Both options are wrong. There's a third. The AI phone calls are already happening. Reuters reported that people using Meta's Muse, the personal AI agent launched in the U.S. this past September, can have it call businesses to book appointments, check inventory or get quotes from contractors. A Meta employee testing this feature said an insurer kept hanging up on Muse after realizing it was an AI caller. At InsureTech Connect in Las Vegas, Steve Rullo, who is Guardian Life's chief digital and technology officer, told Insurance Business , "We are already seeing providers calling in for verification of benefits with AI." He described healthcare providers using AI to verify patient benefits, often for an entire list of patients in a single call. The Debate Is About Websites Since Muse launched, carriers and marketplaces have been deciding whether to allow it access. Insurify quickly blocked Muse, saying it "risks stripping carrier quotes of critical contextual information." Co-CEO Giorgos Zacharia explained, "A quote without its context is not a fair comparison. It is a number." Shortly afterward, Kin announced that it would let Muse crawl its site so customers can shop for quotes , and Zebra announced an integration the following day. Employers, a workers' compensation insurer, told Dig-In it doesn't allow third-party AI agents like Muse to access its operational systems or customer data. Each of those decisions is about access to a website or system. None of them covers phone calls, and blocking Muse online won't stop it from calling. I expect insurers will get a lot more of these calls. Handled the old way, they're a cost. Handled well, every one is a quote in front of a real shopper. That's where the real opportunities are. The Talking Is About 5% of the Value The answer is simple: AI for AI, humans for humans. Let AI answer calls from other AI, and let people answer calls from people. This way, a family dealing with a flooded basement won't be stuck on hold while a licensed agent talks to a bot. Most voice AI answers the phone, then sends the caller through a phone menu or to a person. That's 5% of the value. The other 95% is the work behind the call: pulling up the policy, filing the claim, writing the result back to the core system. If AI can handle a machine caller's request at this level, no person needs to pick up, and licensed people can focus on judgment calls, like denied claims. Most carriers aren't there yet. According to KPMG International's report Unlocking AI value in insurance , only 29% of respondents use AI agents or automation for end-to-end processes. Rullo said Guardian will keep people involved in its AI processes: "We'll still have a human in the loop." For some risk profiles, he said, Guardian wants alerts on exceptions instead of reviews of every transaction. People should own the decisions. They shouldn't have to answer every call. You Can't Always Tell Who Is Calling Carriers also can't always tell if a caller is a machine or a person. Reuters reported that Meta tested having human contractors make some Muse calls without telling the other party. A Meta vice president said the test without proper disclosures "was a miss," and Reuters said Meta has rolled back that test for now. So a call that seems to come from an AI agent might actually be from a person. Zacharia told Dig-In that Muse got around Insurify's bot detection and didn't identify itself. A system designed to resolve requests can help both human and AI callers. A system that only routes calls can't. Policyholders Already Draw the Line In Liberate's September survey of 1,001 U.S. claimants, 50% said they would prefer a claim paid in 60 seconds with no human contact over talking to a person within 10 minutes and getting paid in three days. Another 41% preferred a person on the phone. Of those who chose the fast payout, 55% still want a human involved in every denial. Fast on yes. Human on no. Across the whole survey, 61% say a human must review every denial. In the same survey, 86% want to be told when AI touches their claim. A Hi Marley survey of 550 senior property and casualty decision-makers and 2,000 policyholders in the U.S. and Canada highlights the gap carriers need to close. Eighty-five percent of executives think AI will build customer trust, but only 40% of policyholders agree. Ninety percent of policyholders said it's very or extremely important to know when they're interacting with AI, and two-thirds said their biggest worry is not being able to reach a human when it matters. Three Rules for Carriers First, use insurance-specific AI that works within your core systems to answer calls from machines. Sending a bot to a phone menu or a person wastes time and doesn't solve the problem. Second, keep a licensed person on every denial, no matter what else the AI handles. Third, be transparent about AI on both sides. Let people know when they're talking to AI, and expect AI callers to do the same. If carriers follow these rules, they can answer every call, whether it's from a person or an AI. The shopper using a machine gets a response, and the family with a flooded basement gets to talk to a real person. Insurance has always wanted to answer everyone who calls. Now it can. Amrish Singh

items.title: Insurers Await AI Integration in Core Platforms
items.original_title: Insurers Await AI Integration in Core Platforms
items.rss_title: Insurers Await AI Integration in Core Platforms
items.rss_description: Insurers Await AI Integration in Core Platforms Data Analytics ITL Editorial Team Wed, 10/21/2026 - 13:06 Insurers aren't avoiding AI due to fear—they're waiting for core platform vendors to deliver native capabilities instead of risky integrations. October 22, 2026 Image We've all heard some version of the same story this year: Many carriers and brokers are still on the fence about AI because of regulatory risk, errors and omissions (E&O) exposure, or "black boxes" they can't explain to a state department of insurance (DOI) examiner. All of this is true. But none of it tells the whole story. Spend time with almost any carrier's IT and operations leaders, and eventually they'll say the quiet part out loud: They're not avoiding AI; they're waiting for it to arrive inside the systems they already run. Those systems are the core platforms, such as Duck Creek, Guidewire, Majesco, Sapiens, and Insurity, that sit beneath a large share of the policies and claims on the books today. The Real Bottleneck Isn't Fear. It's Architecture. For most carriers, policy, billing, and claims data live in a core system: a multi-year, multimillion-dollar investment that the business treats as its "single source of truth." The vendor varies from carrier to carrier, but the obstacle their IT teams face is the same. Bolting a standalone AI tool onto that architecture, even an elegant and streamlined one, isn't a plug-and-play decision. It's a multi-team integration project that typically stretches across several quarters, exposing the organization to delays, cost overruns, and shifting priorities. One claims technology vendor estimates that AI vendors lose roughly 40% of their projected timelines to integration complexity, whether the carrier runs Guidewire, Duck Creek, Majesco, or a custom legacy core. That kind of complexity is often the difference between a pilot that launches and one that quietly dies in the backlog. Naturally, carriers also scan the standalone AI market. They see dozens of point solutions for underwriting triage, claims scoring, and first notice of loss (FNOL) intake, and wonder: "Why integrate a third-party layer today when the core vendor is about to deliver the same capabilities natively?" It isn't a hypothetical question. Nearly every major core platform vendor is moving to close this gap. Consider a few examples: Duck Creek launched its Agentic AI Platform in April 2026. That same month, Guidewire embedded ProNavigator, an AI assistant that gives adjusters context-specific guidance, into ClaimCenter and its other core applications. In August, Guidewire followed with its Qusar release, which added Guidewire-built claims and underwriting agents, including an agentic FNOL tool. Majesco announced that it's quadrupling its AI investment in 2026 to build an AI-native P&C platform and expand Majesco Copilot and its agentic AI capabilities. Sapiens has been rolling AI-based functionality into its CoreSuite releases. Insurity has committed an additional $100 million over two years to embed AI in its core systems, on top of the more than $50 million it had already invested in AI and R&D. In each case, the pitch is essentially the same: The AI isn't a separate purchase; it's part of the system carriers already pay for. That point is missing from many of the "why insurers are hesitant" stories in the media. Carriers aren't approaching AI cautiously simply because they're risk-averse. They're using their position as large, long-term platform customers to create a buyer's advantage. That leverage lets them be deliberate about their "build-versus-buy-versus-wait" calculations—and for many carriers, waiting has so far proved the more disciplined option. Why Waiting Is a Deceptively Difficult Decision The problem is that waiting has a cost, too, and that cost doesn't fall evenly. One AI underwriting vendor that sells a core-agnostic product has argued that carriers and managing general agents (MGAs) can't afford to wait for a full core system transformation before deploying AI and can't afford to be locked into a tool that works with only one platform. Both concerns are valid, which makes waiting a strategic bet rather than an obvious answer. There's also a quieter signal that undercuts the "carriers are simply being cautious" narrative. A May 2026 IA Capital Group survey of national and regional carriers found OpenAI's models in 91% of respondents' AI stacks, often delivered through Microsoft Copilot. Carriers aren't AI-averse. They're AI-selective, using their scale to adopt productivity tools quickly while holding the line on systems of record until their core vendors catch up. For many of them, that moment has either arrived or is very close. The Exception That Proves the Rule So why do carriers buy standalone tools at all? Because when a tool solves a problem that general-purpose AI, or the AI now arriving in core platforms, doesn't handle well, the calculus flips. That's where most insurance-specific AI vendors stake their pitch: not "we're AI," but "we're AI trained on insurance data and workflows, which a horizontal model wrapped around your files isn't." It's an argument that still holds water. Shift Technology has made this case to carrier IT leaders directly, arguing that generic horizontal AI players often lack the data foundations and expertise needed to move a pilot into production. It's a real distinction, not just positioning. A general-purpose model can summarize a claims file. Reasoning reliably across coverage language, state-specific regulations, and loss histories is a different problem, and it's one that a system trained specifically on that data is, at least in theory, built to solve. What sustains the "insurance-specific always beats generic" argument, then? The products carriers keep buying from these vendors, despite their preference for waiting until such capabilities arrive inside a core system, share one trait: They're widely believed to do the job better because of deep domain training, proprietary data, or a workflow too specialized for a core vendor to prioritize anytime soon. Everything else, such as a general chat interface bolted onto a claims queue, is the kind of functionality most likely to show up natively in the next core release, whichever vendor delivers it. That's why carriers aren't rushing to pay for it twice. What This Means If You're Evaluating Tools Right Now A few things are worth doing before you sign anything: Separating "edge" AI from "core" AI. Marketing copy and service-desk triage carry low regulatory exposure and can run successfully on general-purpose tools today. Underwriting and claims determinations that touch policyholder outcomes are a different risk category, where the wait-for-native instinct makes more sense. Asking vendors for proof of successful integrations, not just a demo. A clean demo says nothing about how a tool behaves once it's wired into a decade-old core system. Ask for a named carrier reference on your exact platform and version. Pushing for a real audit trail. If a vendor can't produce output in a format that your internal compliance team and state DOI examiners would accept, that's a governance gap that will surface at the worst possible time. Ensuring pilot programs don't require a multi-year lock-in. Any AI vendor worth considering should be comfortable running a three- to six-month pilot on a limited book of business before asking for a long-term commitment. Watching your core vendor's product roadmap as closely as the pitch deck. If your platform vendor plans to deliver the capability you're evaluating in its next release cycle, that changes the decision, even if the standalone tool works well today. Testing whether the value is domain-specific. James Ballot Diane Brassard October 22, 2026 We've all heard some version of the same story this year: Many carriers and brokers are still on the fence about AI because of regulatory risk, errors and omissions (E&O) exposure, or "black boxes" they can't explain to a state department of insurance (DOI) examiner. All of this is true. But none of it tells the whole story. Spend time with almost any carrier's IT and operations leaders, and eventually they'll say the quiet part out loud: They're not avoiding AI they're waiting for it to arrive inside the systems they already run. Those systems are the core platforms, such as Duck Creek, Guidewire, Majesco, Sapiens, and Insurity, that sit beneath a large share of the policies and claims on the books today. The Real Bottleneck Isn't Fear. It's Architecture. For most carriers, policy, billing, and claims data live in a core system: a multi-year, multimillion-dollar investment that the business treats as its "single source of truth." The vendor varies from carrier to carrier, but the obstacle their IT teams face is the same. Bolting a standalone AI tool onto that architecture, even an elegant and streamlined one, isn't a plug-and-play decision. It's a multi-team integration project that typically stretches across several quarters, exposing the organization to delays, cost overruns, and shifting priorities. One claims technology vendor estimates that AI vendors lose roughly 40% of their projected timelines to integration complexity, whether the carrier runs Guidewire, Duck Creek, Majesco, or a custom legacy core. That kind of complexity is often the difference between a pilot that launches and one that quietly dies in the backlog. Naturally, carriers also scan the standalone AI market. They see dozens of point solutions for underwriting triage, claims scoring, and first notice of loss (FNOL) intake, and wonder: "Why integrate a third-party layer today when the core vendor is about to deliver the same capabilities natively?" It isn't a hypothetical question. Nearly every major core platform vendor is moving to close this gap. Consider a few examples: Duck Creek launched its Agentic AI Platform in April 2026. That same month, Guidewire embedded ProNavigator, an AI assistant that gives adjusters context-specific guidance, into ClaimCenter and its other core applications. In August, Guidewire followed with its Qusar release, which added Guidewire-built claims and underwriting agents, including an agentic FNOL tool. Majesco announced that it's quadrupling its AI investment in 2026 to build an AI-native P&C platform and expand Majesco Copilot and its agentic AI capabilities. Sapiens has been rolling AI-based functionality into its CoreSuite releases. Insurity has committed an additional $100 million over two years to embed AI in its core systems, on top of the more than $50 million it had already invested in AI and R&D. In each case, the pitch is essentially the same: The AI isn't a separate purchase it's part of the system carriers already pay for. That point is missing from many of the "why insurers are hesitant" stories in the media. Carriers aren't approaching AI cautiously simply because they're risk-averse. They're using their position as large, long-term platform customers to create a buyer's advantage. That leverage lets them be deliberate about their "build-versus-buy-versus-wait" calculations—and for many carriers, waiting has so far proved the more disciplined option. Why Waiting Is a Deceptively Difficult Decision The problem is that waiting has a cost, too, and that cost doesn't fall evenly. One AI underwriting vendor that sells a core-agnostic product has argued that carriers and managing general agents (MGAs) can't afford to wait for a full core system transformation before deploying AI and can't afford to be locked into a tool that works with only one platform. Both concerns are valid, which makes waiting a strategic bet rather than an obvious answer. There's also a quieter signal that undercuts the "carriers are simply being cautious" narrative. A May 2026 IA Capital Group survey of national and regional carriers found OpenAI's models in 91% of respondents' AI stacks, often delivered through Microsoft Copilot. Carriers aren't AI-averse. They're AI-selective, using their scale to adopt productivity tools quickly while holding the line on systems of record until their core vendors catch up. For many of them, that moment has either arrived or is very close. The Exception That Proves the Rule So why do carriers buy standalone tools at all? Because when a tool solves a problem that general-purpose AI, or the AI now arriving in core platforms, doesn't handle well, the calculus flips. That's where most insurance-specific AI vendors stake their pitch: not "we're AI," but "we're AI trained on insurance data and workflows, which a horizontal model wrapped around your files isn't." It's an argument that still holds water. Shift Technology has made this case to carrier IT leaders directly, arguing that generic horizontal AI players often lack the data foundations and expertise needed to move a pilot into production. It's a real distinction, not just positioning. A general-purpose model can summarize a claims file. Reasoning reliably across coverage language, state-specific regulations, and loss histories is a different problem, and it's one that a system trained specifically on that data is, at least in theory, built to solve. What sustains the "insurance-specific always beats generic" argument, then? The products carriers keep buying from these vendors, despite their preference for waiting until such capabilities arrive inside a core system, share one trait: They're widely believed to do the job better because of deep domain training, proprietary data, or a workflow too specialized for a core vendor to prioritize anytime soon. Everything else, such as a general chat interface bolted onto a claims queue, is the kind of functionality most likely to show up natively in the next core release, whichever vendor delivers it. That's why carriers aren't rushing to pay for it twice. Marketing copy and service-desk triage carry low regulatory exposure and can run successfully on general-purpose tools today. Underwriting and claims determinations that touch policyholder outcomes are a different risk category, where the wait-for-native instinct makes more sense. Asking vendors for proof of successful integrations, not just a demo. A clean demo says nothing about how a tool behaves once it's wired into a decade-old core system. Ask for a named carrier reference on your exact platform and version. Pushing for a real audit trail. If a vendor can't produce output in a format that your internal compliance team and state DOI examiners would accept, that's a governance gap that will surface at the worst possible time. Ensuring pilot programs don't require a multi-year lock-in. Any AI vendor worth considering should be comfortable running a three- to six-month pilot on a limited book of business before asking for a long-term commitment. Watching your core vendor's product roadmap as closely as the pitch deck. If your platform vendor plans to deliver the capability you're evaluating in its next release cycle, that changes the decision, even if the standalone tool works well today. If a vendor's edge could be replicated by connecting a general-purpose model (for example, an enterprise assistant such as Microsoft Copilot, or an AI workflow that retrieves and summarizes documents) to your own policy forms, endorsements, claim files, and underwriting guidelines, don't count on that edge lasting once your core system catches up. items.rss_title: Need an Idea for Innovation? How About 1,208,580?
items.rss_description: Need an Idea for Innovation? How About 1,208,580? PaulCarroll Mon, 10/26/2026 - 17:11 Bill Gross recently announced a free database of AI-generated ideas for innovative companies, based on the 31 methodologies that he's developed over the past three decades and that have powered his Idealab incubator. The list of ideas — currently totaling a whopping 1,208,580 — may or may not contain an idea that you'll be able to turn into big bucks, but I think that exploring the database and interacting with the ideas is worth a bit of your time. Many of the notions I see for the insurance market are provocative. They can at least suggest where there are holes in insurance offerings today that you should work to fill, even if you don't launch the sort of standalone company that Gross would love to see join his pioneering incubator. Let's have a look. Here is a link to the database . And here is a link to a Fortune article that describes the effort in detail, including Gross's argument that innovations driven by AI will create far more jobs than it will eliminate. The article says Gross's prompts to the AI break down into three categories: "O pportunities, which he says are things such as solving a business pain point, removing friction, removing waste, removing danger, and improving design, among others; enablers, such as new technologies, scientific advances, and new materials, processes, or changing cost curves that make solutions more feasible than before; and shifts, such as regulatory changes, as well as behavioral, economic, cultural, or geopolitical movements that make the timing for a particular business seem right. " Gross also fed his AI " some 17 million source documents that included news stories, research reports, expired patents, public company filings, and threads from online community discussion boards" and came up with his 1.2 million ideas for new businesses. But are the ideas any good? I certainly found them thought-provoking. For instance, I selected the "fintech/insurtech" option, specified that I didn't want to invest more than $250,000, wanted to get to market within a year and hoped to "make the insurance claims process smoother for customers." The top suggestion, which the AI suggested was a 57% fit for me, was for a "claims trust operating system that... gives policyholders visibility into the evidence shaping settlements and repairs." I'm not sure that's a business. It would take an awful lot of work to assemble the huge amount of settlement and repair data that would be needed to be truly definitive, but the idea raises an intriguing notion: Somebody will surely try to use an AI to give policyholders a quick handle on what the insurer will likely offer after a car accident, water damage to a home, etc. If the insurance industry provides the initial take, it will be able to lower expectations and control payments. If plaintiff attorneys fill the need, they'll be able to raise expectations, influencing policyholders to be disappointed... and perhaps hire an attorney to contest the offer. The competing interests would seem to create an opportunity for a trusted intermediary, but I, at least, have become skeptical about whether it could stay unbiased. I subscribe to the notion laid out by Cory Doctorow in a seminal blog post republished by Wired magazine in 2023 that describes the process of — excuse my French — enshittification. As I wrote at the time , Amazon is a great example. It initially built a huge base of customers by doing everything possible to make life simple for them. Once it had the customer base, it courted businesses — and the customer experience started to get gunked up by ads, attempts to keep customers from easily finding the best deals, etc. Once Amazon had built a marketplace where companies had to have a presence, it started milking them as much as possible on behalf of investors — a fee here, a fee there, maybe Amazon would even use its insights into sales data to launch products or businesses that would undercut a company with a hit offering on Amazon's platform. (Amazon has consistently denied doing so but has faced many lawsuits alleging it does.) Just about everybody still uses Amazon, but the experience is very different than it was a decade ago. Even if I'm right that there isn't a business in a "claims trust operating system," the Idealab database has still pointed to a sore spot that the insurance industry needs to address. Somebody is going to use AI to shape policyholders' thinking about what to expect as a settlement, by providing near-instant estimates. So insurers should at least be thinking about how they show their work, and quickly, to keep plaintiff attorneys from setting unrealistic expectations and accelerating the trend toward more and more litigation. So I'd recommend that, whatever your role in the insurance ecosystem, you poke around in the database to see what friction points and opportunities it has surfaced that you might be able to address. There are more ideas than I can count about underwriting, pricing, services from agents and brokers, and on and on. If you're like me, your eyes glaze over after half an hour or so of an exercise like this, so maybe make a visit to the database an occasional excursion over the next month, perhaps at the end of the day as you're winding down or before a weekly meeting with colleagues so you can stir up discussions. We all get locked into our mindsets and into our day-to-day routines, and Gross has provided a whole host of prompts that can challenge us to do ever more than we are now. Cheers, Paul Image Paul Carroll The founder of Idealab has used AI to generate more than 1.2 million ideas for innovative AI-based companies, including in insurance. They're thought-provoking. items.extracted_text: Nephila Capital ILS fund revenues keep rising, even as soft market evident in fronted premium - Artemis.bm Nephila Capital ILS fund revenues keep rising, even as soft market evident in fronted premium - Artemis.bm Nephila Capital ILS fund revenues keep rising, even as soft market evident in fronted premium 29th October 2026 - Author: Steve Evans Nephila Capital’s insurance-linked securities (ILS) fund management business continues to deliver in 2026, as revenues reported within parent Markel’s quarterly results showed yet another increase of nearly 40% to $42.2 million for the third-quarter, even as the soft reinsurance market becomes increasingly evident in the volume of premiums fronted to Nephila’s reinsurers. After the first-quarter of this year, Nephila Capital’s insurance-linked securities fund management revenues had risen by an impressive 59% year-on-year, to reach $40.5 million for Q1 2026 . Then, for the second-quarter, ILS fund management revenues generated by Nephila Capital reached $37.7 million, a 23% increase on Q2 2025’s $29.1 million, while the first-half 2026 total reported of $78.1 million was a 30% increase over H1 2025’s ILS fund revenues of $54.6 million earned by the Nephila Capital business. Over the course of the first nine months of 2026, Nephila Capital has now generated $120.3 million in ILS fund management revenues for its parent Markel, an almost 42% increase year-on-year from $85 million by the end of September 2025. The third-quarter of the year is likely a period where more performance fees have an effect for Nephila’s business, given the seasonal premium accrual that benefits reinsurance contracts at that time of year. This naturally suggests the investors backing Nephila’s range of ILS fund strategies will have been seeing positive returns all year, given how the fund management revenues have been rising. This trend has been persistent through the last year or so, for ILS related earnings to be increasing over the prior year quarters, as Nephila Capital has naturally benefited from the higher inward rates it had been earning from underwriting business of recent years, the way it has been able to leverage its underwriting using its infrastructure to write more premium, as well as the more benign major catastrophe loss environment. But, with property catastrophe reinsurance rates now softened and that expected to persist into 2027, it will be interesting to see how ILS management fee income related earnings adjust through 2027, for Nephila Capital and other players in the space. Nephila Capital’s premium volumes assumed via the fronted programs operated through parent Markel’s business infrastructure fell again in the third-quarter of 2026. The trend of Nephila’s reinsurance entities assuming more premiums through these fronted programs began to reverse in recent quarters, as Markel said rate decreases reduce the volumes. Recall that, in full-year 2025, Markel fronted 42% more in gross premiums for Nephila entities and ILS structures , as the manager expanded its stature further in the reinsurance market. But then through quarters in 2026, the softening pricing in the catastrophe reinsurance market has meant these fronted premium volumes have fallen behind the prior year. For the third-quarter of 2026, Markel reported $58.5 million of premium was ceded to Nephila’s reinsurers, down from $162.9 million in Q3 2025. Year-to-date in 2026, the figure stood at $1.1 billion by September 30th, again a decline from 9-month 2025’s $1.8 billion. Markel again cited “lower premiums on our property catastrophe programs with Nephila driven by rate decreases.” However, while the softer market pricing in reinsurance is a factor, there is another to consider as Nephila has other fronting arrangements in place which could account for at least some of the decline. As we had reported, Nephila also struck up a fronting relationship with Enstar and utilised its Cavello Bay reinsurer entity to front risk for it this year, first seen in Florida Citizens reinsurance placement . As Nephila looks to diversify its routes to market, including fronting partnerships, we may find it more of a challenge to know just how much of the premium decline reported by Markel is actually due to the soft market pricing and how much may be due to certain reinsurance deals being fronted elsewhere. The reinsurance recoverable due from Nephila Capital’s reinsurance entities that Markel reports on its balance sheet has declined further, continuing to reflect the effect of commutations made and losses being realised from the past, as we saw begin to take effect in 2025 . The reinsurance recoverables due to Markel from Nephila reinsurers had fallen to $241.9 million by June 30th 2026, but by September 30th had declined further to a recent historical low of $187.2 million. It seems that Nephila Capital may have increased some of its hedging arrangements in the third-quarter, as Markel reported that fronted ceding reinsurance contracts for industry-loss warranty (ILW) or other retrocession arrangements for the Nephila reinsurers were $18.8 million of gross premiums in Q3 2026, up on the prior year’s $7 million. Year-to-date, Markel reported that gross premiums written through fronted ceded reinsurance contracts, primarily in the form of industry loss warranties, had reached $36.8 million by September 30th, down from $81.5 million for 9-months 2025. Markel cited the “higher management fees for our insurance-linked securities investment management services” in commenting on the results for its financial segment, which contains the Nephila Capital and State National businesses. The Nephila Capital business remains a source of attractive and diversified income for Markel, being the only business unit with a reinsurance underwriting focus these days. Nephila Capital had increased its third-party assets under management to $7.9 billion as of June 30th 2026 . Markel also reported in its Q3 results that it has entered into an adverse development cover reinsurance agreement with Cavello Bay, Enstar’s reinsurer, to cover subject reserves totalling $4.8 billion from its run-off Global Reinsurance business and some exited lines within its insurance operations. (Series 2027-1) catastrophe bond transaction to provide it with $300 million of collateralized multi-peril retrocession, while the price guidance on the notes has been lowered, Artemis has learned. Hamilton Insurance Group, the Bermuda based insurance and reinsurance holding company, returned to the catastrophe bond market earlier this month with an initial target to secure $250 million of protection from this Easton Re 2027-1 offering . The company’s $200 million Easton Re Ltd. (Series 2024-1) cat bond is scheduled to mature early next year, making this new offering appear to be a renewal of sorts and now a meaningful upsizing of that coverage. This 2027-1 issuance is set to be the third 144A catastrophe bond offering under the Easton Re name for Hamilton’s reinsurance entity Hamilton Re , while the company has also sponsored a private cat bond prior to those deals. We won’t repeat all the details of the cat bond in our updates on size and pricing, so be sure to visit the Deal Directory entry for more background on the transaction . Easton Re Ltd. is now offering cat bond investors a single $300 million Class A tranche of Series 2027-1 notes, upsized from the initial $250 million, to provide Hamilton Re and Hamilton subsidiaries with industry-loss trigger and per-occurrence retro protection against U.S., DC, Puerto Rico, and Virgin Islands named storms, as well as U.S. and Canada earthquakes, over a three year term. The now $300 million of Series 2027-1 Class A notes that Easton Re is offering come with an initial expected loss of 2.66% and were first offered to cat bond investors with spread price guidance in a range from 4.75% to 5.25%. That price guidance has now been lowered to a revised range of 4% to 4.75%, we are told. It’s good to see Hamilton looking to build on its catastrophe bond protection even more, while the decline in pricing is no surprise given how cat bond issues have been executing of late with the market well-capitalised and fund managers having cash to deploy. items.rss_description: Buy or Build? Yes. Data Analytics ITL Editorial Team Fri, 10/23/2026 - 13:49 AI has lowered barriers to building custom insurance workflows, but integration and adoption remain the hardest parts of implementation. October 26, 2026 Image One of my takeaways from ITC Vegas this fall was that a lot of vendors are playing defense. A lot of carriers are looking at what AI can do now and asking some version of the same question: Hold on a minute, the world changed, so should we just build everything ourselves? It's a fair question. The barriers to building have come down a lot in the last year, and the benefits of owning your own technology are real. When a convincing demo takes a couple of engineers instead of a sales cycle, the old reasons to buy start to look pretty thin. I suppose I'm not the most neutral person to ask. I've spent the last decade building and running Clearcover , an AI-native carrier, and now Dearborn Labs , an AI-native software development firm built specifically for insurance; if anyone was going to tell you to build everything, it would probably be me. But when people ask me whether to buy or build, my answer is...yes. We have components of our system that we bought and didn't build, and we're fine with that. We build more than we buy, though, and more every day. Is "yes" a dodge? Maybe a little. Mostly it's that buy vs. build was never one decision. Every carrier already runs a mix of both, workflow by workflow. And even the build half of my answer comes with an asterisk. Where should the line sit? The choices sit along a spectrum, made one workflow at a time, and lately the mix has been shifting toward build. That makes sense to me, and I'd expect it to keep shifting for as long as building keeps getting cheaper. Buy what's already solved well. If a problem looks roughly the same at every carrier, and someone has spent years getting good at it, there isn't much to gain from building your own version, and the time and money are better spent elsewhere. But that list gets shorter every month. Build the workflows where being different is the point, like how you triage a new claim or decide which risks to write. Buying those means working the same way as everyone else who bought the same thing, which probably isn't what you were going for. Where exactly that line falls depends a lot on the carrier and its lines of business, which is why a single company-wide decision on buy vs. build usually ends up wrong somewhere. The asterisk What qualifies as building, because you can put a demo together, is usually the smallest portion of the work. AI can change how a claim moves and which decisions get made without a person ever opening the file, but the systems underneath that workflow rarely change, or at least they rarely change quickly. Not everybody is doing a rip-and-replace of their whole company to launch a new AI workflow. A new claims-intake workflow still has to post to your core system and set reserves the way your actuaries expect, and an underwriting workbench still has to read from policy admin and write its decisions back. None of that shows up in a demo. The interface is mostly a solved problem now, and that's good news. The hard part is the wiring underneath it. Most of the AI conversations I have with carriers wind up being about traditional software engineering. That's the work of fitting whatever the AI application or agent is into the rest of the company, so the systems supporting a reinvented workflow still work properly. And the wiring is only half of the asterisk. The other half is running the thing in production until people actually work that way. Most implementation projects are scoped to end at go-live, which is roughly where this half starts. At Clearcover, adoption of the AI tools across our claims team is 92%+. A number like that gets earned after go-live, inside real claims, over however long it takes for the new way of working to become just how the job gets done. You might reasonably ask whether all of this is an argument for buying something that comes already integrated. For the work that's solved well, it is. But a bought workflow is the vendor's workflow, designed to fit as many carriers as possible, and in the workflows you'd want to run differently from everyone else, that's exactly the problem. Build realistically. Before you build a new workflow, ask three questions of it: Foundation — Was this workflow designed around constraints that no longer exist? Fit — Can it work with the systems you already have, without a rip and replace? Engineering — Do your engineers own the integration layer today, and can you test, govern and audit what runs on it? The first is about not building on top of a bad foundation. A lot of insurance workflows were shaped by limits that made sense at the time, like a handoff that existed because two systems couldn't talk to each other, or a sampling audit that existed because nobody could read every file. If you automate that workflow as it stands, what you get is the old process running a little faster, and you've spent real money to keep a constraint you no longer have. The second one is more encouraging. You don't have to fully rip out your systems to improve a workflow, so long as you have the software engineering chops to fit the new workflow into the systems you have. The third is the one I'd push on hardest, mostly because a demo is very good at hiding it. If the answer is no, I'd want to know that before the demo goes in front of the Board rather than after. If you're asking me whether to buy or build, I'd say build more than you used to. Just go in knowing that the demo is the easy part, and that the wiring, plus the long stretch of running it until people actually work that way, is the job. So where does your line sit this year, and who's doing the wiring? Kyle Nakatsuji

The GAM Swiss Re ILS Income NZ PIE Fund launches as a fund strategy sitting within the GAM Investment Funds PIE Scheme and is designed to provide New Zealand investors with an efficient route to access the returns of a global portfolio of insurance-linked securities (ILS), primarily catastrophe bonds, in an NZD-hedged format. The PIE strategy will invest substantially all of its assets in the NZD hedged share class of the GAM Swiss Re Cat Bond, which is the long-standing Irish-domiciled UCITS cat bond fund that was launched in 2011. Investors into a PIE fund strategy in New Zealand can benefit from a comparably lower tax rate rather than investing directly into the underlying offshore fund. “We are pleased to bring this strategy to New Zealand. The PIE structure gives advisers and their clients access to an established ILS fund in a format designed for local investors, with currency exposure hedged to the New Zealand dollar,” explained Eric Finnell, GAM’s Managing Director, Australia and New Zealand. The master fund, the GAM Swiss Re Cat Bond UCITS strategy, that underlies the GAM Swiss Re ILS Income NZ PIE Fund is co-managed by GAM London Limited and Swiss Re Insurance-Linked Strategies Inc., the specialist ILS investment management unit of the global reinsurance firm. That GAM Swiss Re Cat Bond UCITS Fund had expanded its assets under management (AUM) in 2026, reaching $2.03 billion as of August 4th , and as of today just over $2.08 billion. GAM has partnered with Adminis, a New Zealand based technology-driven wealth solutions specialist, to issue and manage its cat bond fund in the country in the PIE format. Adminis provides investment accounting, administration, custody, registry, and portfolio and performance reporting services, supporting fund managers looking to operate in the New Zealand market. The GAM Swiss Re ILS Income NZ PIE Fund will have a minimum investment size of NZD 50,000 and its initial distribution will be focused on financial advisers and wholesale investors. The fund will be priced weekly and is expected to pay quarterly distributions to investors. Currently the fund will deliver returns based on a portfolio of over 300 securities, substantially catastrophe bonds, that cover event risks globally. By making the GAM Swiss Re Cat Bond investment fund available in a PIE format, GAM and Swiss Re broaden their distribution into New Zealand in an investor friendly format for allocators in that country. It’s not the first catastrophe bond fund in the PIE format, as recall that Fermat Capital Management launched the Fermat Cat Bond PIE Fund back in August , becoming the first cat bond strategy to adopt this distribution route. items.rss_title: Canada’s Biggest Banks Move to Limit AI Agents, Citing Risk

items.extracted_text: Canada’s Biggest Banks Move to Limit AI Agents, Citing Risk Article 0 Comments Some of Canada’s biggest banks are moving to restrict third-party artificial intelligence agents such as Meta Platform Inc.’s Muse from accessing their banking systems, citing security and liability risks. Royal Bank of Canada, the country’s largest lender, sent a message to all employees Tuesday informing them of the policy change, noting it came after a “full security review of the technology and its functionality,” and that it follows the company’s guidelines on responsible use of AI, according to a memo seen by Bloomberg. On Wednesday, Bank of Montreal, Toronto-Dominion Bank and Bank of Nova Scotia said they are also restricting third-party agents from accessing their digital banking systems. Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce said it does “not support personal AI agents directly opening or accessing accounts,” while a spokesperson for National Bank of Canada said it’s “closely monitoring” the issue and still assessing the opportunities for clients and potential risks. The RBC note was sent by Naim Kazmi, group head of technology and operations, and Erica Nielsen, group head of personal banking. Bank spokesperson Jeff Lanthier confirmed its contents. “After careful consideration and based on what we know today, RBC has made the decision to block third-party personal AI agents from direct access to authenticated RBC digital properties,” Kazmi and Nielsen said, adding that they know that such agents “accessing banking systems can create unacceptable customer risk, including acting beyond customer expectations or creating liability exposure.” Lanthier said the bank recognizes this may disappoint the “small portion of our clients who use these tools,” but added the decision was taken based on the “safety and security of our clients and systems.” Several US banks have blocked or restricted unauthorized outside AI agents from accessing customer accounts or moving money. Earlier this month, Charles Schwab Corp. Chief Executive Officer Rick Wurster said his company is actively blocking unauthorized AI agents attempting to move clients’ money. In an interview with Bloomberg Television last week, RBC CEO Dave McKay said the lender was considering blocking Muse from accessing customer information. Many of the other Canadian banks said they’re interested in the value AI innovation can deliver for clients but also expressed concern about the loss of sensitive data. Several urged their customers not to share their banking credentials with AI agents. “To protect our clients, BMO does not permit AI agents to access our digital properties or execute transactions,” spokesperson Jeff Roman said. Ada Lovelace Rampersaud, a representative for Toronto-Dominion, said the firm “has made the decision to block all third-party personal AI agents from direct access to banking information, where authentication is required, while we ensure the appropriate safeguards, authorization mechanisms and oversight are in place.” A Scotiabank representative said that it was limiting third-party AI agents and will “closely monitor evolving concerns.” Photograph: The Royal Bank of Canada (RBC) building in the financial district of Toronto, Ontario, Canada, on Monday, July 20, 2026 photo credit: Adetona Omokanye/Bloomberg Copyright 2026 Bloomberg. items.original_title: LA Wildfire Smoke Exposed 7 Million to Dangerous Toxic Metals
items.rss_title: LA Wildfire Smoke Exposed 7 Million to Dangerous Toxic Metals
items.rss_description: A catastrophic 2025 Los Angeles firestorm exposed some 7 million people to high levels of airborne lead and other toxic metals released from burning homes and vehicles, according to a new study. Scientists for the first time were able to …
items.extracted_text: LA Wildfire Smoke Exposed 7 Million to Dangerous Toxic Metals Article 0 Comments A catastrophic 2025 Los Angeles firestorm exposed some 7 million people to high levels of airborne lead and other toxic metals released from burning homes and vehicles, according to a new study. Scientists for the first time were able to quantify in real time the chemical composition of wildfire smoke thanks to a sensor network that went online months before the January 2025 Eaton conflagration that destroyed more than 9,400 buildings, killing 19 people. Related: Will California’s New Smoke Claims Law Create a Recovery Bottleneck? As climate change triggers urban firestorms like the inferno in the LA suburb of Altadena, the paper published Wednesday in the journal Science Advances offers the first indication of how the incineration of homes, electronics, cars and infrastructure could affect even people who live far from the burn zone due to wind-blown toxic smoke. The researchers determined that over a 24-hour period, smoke from the fire contained 80 times the concentration of lead normally found in the atmosphere. Lead is a neurotoxin linked to an array of health effects and is particularly harmful to children. Sensors also detected highly elevated levels of arsenic and other toxins. The smoke plume covered eastern LA and the San Gabriel Valley and affected about 70% of the county’s population. Nga Lee (Sally) Ng, a co-author of the study and a professor of environmental science and engineering at the California Institute of Technology, said that while chronic exposure to metals like lead is well-studied, the health effects from short-term exposure to highly concentrated airborne toxins remains largely unknown. “The hope is that with these real-time measurements, we can better understand and characterize the health impacts of these short-term exposures,” she said. The data on Eaton was collected by a Los Angeles monitoring site that happened to be downwind of the fire. It’s part of the Atmospheric Science and Chemistry Measurement Network (ASCENT) that has established stations across the country. Ng, who is a principal investigator for the National Science Foundation-funded project, said the LA site wasn’t able to collect data on the Palisades fire, which ignited 34 miles away from the Eaton site hours earlier, due to the wind direction. Related: Edison Drops on Willful Misconduct Allegations in Eaton Fire Case ASCENT also allowed the researchers to track how the toxic composition of the smoke plume changed over time as the fire burned, according to Haroula Baliaka, the study’s lead author who was a PhD candidate at Caltech at the time. That could help health researchers pinpoint health impacts from urban firestorms. She said the study results should encourage policymakers to rethink strategies for evacuating residents from urban wildfires, given toxic smoke exposure can occur far from the burn zone. “I can envision that in the future we have these evacuation zones for smoke exposure as well,” said Baliaka. “Unfortunately, this is not a one-time event. It’s a new reality and we need to adapt to it and we need to do it sooner rather than later.” Top photo: A fallen street light on the road during the Eaton Fire in Altadena, California, on Wednesday, Jan. 8, 2025. items.extracted_text: Yellow Furball Mascot Liberty Biberty Sparks ‘Beautiful’ Protest. Seriously? Article 0 Comments Last Sunday afternoon, a social media driven “protest” against Liberty Mutual Insurance Co.’s fuzzy yellow mascot Liberty Biberty drew several dozen people to the company’s downtown Boston headquarters, according to the Boston Globe . “This is a revolution, this is the next Boston Tea Party,” proclaimed the organizer of the event, Connor Harvey, a New Hampshire resident who a few weeks earlier had posted a rant against the “weird yellow furball” Biberty on a YouTube page called Death of Mascots under the name DimesAreTasty. In his rant that attracted 13,200 views, Harvey called Biberty “the worst mascot of all time” that has “taken over our screens faster than we can stop it.” The new Liberty Mutual ads have appeared on social media and across television including on high-profile sports programs. A few weeks later, Harvey followed up with the invitation to the Sunday “protest” to urge the insurer to pull the ads: “Join us on Sunday, October 25th at 2PM, outside of Liberty Mutual’s global headquarters, where we will protest against Liberty Biberty, the companies’ new disgusting mascot that has plagued our world for the last few months. He is awful and unacceptable, and the people need to make their voices heard.” The announcement of the event garnered more than 600,00 views. Harvey streamed his event live and, as promised, it was peaceful. “I guess people had to do something on a nice autumn day and there was no Patriots game. But this reaction is an advertising person’s dream,” one Boston Globe reader posted about the Sunday protest. Pro and Con Harvey’s online rant against Liberty Biberty has attracted more than 850 comments, pro and con. “Liberty Mutual is that one friend who says a joke that gets laughs once and then never stops making the exact same joke even when people start groaning at it,” stated one. “I thought he was a pineapple,” quipped another. “I would buy their insurance if they burned it in a commercial,” promised another. Some comments are positive. “I actually like Limu Emu and Doug, but I’m completely on board with Liberty,” offered one. “I actually like what Liberty Biberty represents artistically as a practical puppet crafted by the Jim Henson Creature Shop instead of a CGI monstrosity like a lot of companies are doing now. It’s the opposite of slop,” proclaimed another. Still others expressed mixed feelings. “I’m one of the like only people that liked Limu Emu (and Doug), so to see the ad entirely dedicated to replacing Doug and only Doug felt bad,” confessed one. Many used the opportunity as an invitation to discuss other favorite and not-so-favorite mascots/spokespersons, from Cap’n Crunch to Jake from State Farm and Two Guys in Sonic and Jiffy Lube ads to GEICO’s gecko. Comedian John Oliver has also taken to complaining about the new mascot, urging viewers of his HBO Max show Last Week Tonight to post sexualized images of Liberty Biberty on social media to bring about an end to the campaign. Liberty Biberty’s Beginning The new ad campaign that launched in July was developed by Liberty Mutual and its New York creative agency Bandits & Friends. The puppet mascot was crafted by Jim Henson’s Creature Shop to be in the words of the insurer’s press release “the embodiment of the warm, fuzzy feeling you get when you have great coverage at a great price.” Liberty Mutual, Bandits & Friends, and Jim Henson’s Creature Shop have not replied to requests for comment. But the insurer and ad agency explained their thinking at the launch of the campaign in July. The Liberty Biberty character’s roots date back to a 2019 ad in which an actor struggling to pronounce the company name calls it Liberty Biberty, which the insurer says has become a very popular phrase. The new mascot reflects the decision to try to turn the familiarity with that gaffe into a brand asset and lovable mascot. “Liberty Biberty was already hugely culturally relevant, and we saw this untapped potential as an opportunity for the brand to capitalize on,” said Nicholas Bauman, creative director at Bandits & Friends. “So, we turned a flubbed line into an entity in and of itself, while tying it back to Liberty Mutual. And a fuzzy, yellow manifestation of the feeling of great insurance made perfect sense to us.” “Liberty Biberty gives us a fresh way to show up in culture while staying true to what makes Liberty Mutual distinctive,” said Jenna Lebel, Liberty Mutual chief marketing officer. In an interview with Advertising Week just weeks after the launch, Lebel said her team considered “a number of concepts, well over a hundred ads,” before they chose this approach with the fuzzy yellow puppet. “But once we committed to building on the ‘Liberty Biberty’ phrase itself, the character almost had to be something other than a literal person or animal.” She said they wanted something that felt both familiar and unexpected. “The name gives you the familiar. The character gives you the unexpected,” she said. She called the early response “really encouraging” and said the level of early press and social conversation was exceeding expectations. “We’re already seeing strong brand association and likeability in early consumer research. People notice him, and they connect him to Liberty Mutual quickly, which is exactly what you want from a new character in his first weeks,” she told Advertising Week. The campaign was designed to complement existing character-led creative, like LiMu Emu & Doug, rather than replace it. ‘Beautiful Thing’ Reached the day after his Boston “revolution,” Harvey said he is pleased with how his Sunday played out. “Lots of people came out to share their disdain for Liberty Biberty and it looks like a lot of people had fun,” he told Insurance Journal. As for whether it will have any effect on Liberty Mutual, he said he hopes it does but realizes the company “probably dumped millions of dollars into creating this horrible abomination and it would look really bad to the investors if they had to cancel the campaign.” However, he added, “at the end of the day people have a genuine disgust for the mascot, and the longer they keep him around the more people will hate the company and not use their insurance.” The best part of the event for him was “just getting people out of their houses and off their phones to come together…” He said he had multiple people tell him that it was their first protest. That, he said, is “a beautiful thing.” Was this article valuable? Yes No Here are more articles you may enjoy. items.title: Captive owners find new ways to finance risks, manage losses
items.original_title: Captive owners find new ways to finance risks, manage losses
items.rss_title: Captive owners find new ways to finance risks, manage losses
items.rss_description: Captive insurance companies are increasingly used for more than traditional risk financing, as owners seek to improve loss prevention, manage capital more efficiently and extend insurance services to business partners.
items.extracted_text: Some companies use captive loss data to guide investments in property maintenance and security, while others develop sophisticated investment strategies to support long-tail liabilities or ensure that risk management aligns with the parent company’s strategy. In addition, some established captive owners are restructuring their captives to accommodate risks from vendors, customers and joint ventures, speakers said Wednesday at the Vermont Captive Insurance Association’s Chicago Chapter Summit. One emerging trend is the conversion of single-parent captives into sponsored captives, which allow other organizations to insure their risks through segregated cells, said Christine Brown, deputy commissioner of captive insurance at the Vermont Department of Financial Regulation. Under the structures, captive owners can offer risk management services to business partners and collect fees while keeping the partners’ risks separate from their own, she said. The structures can also accommodate joint venture risks that companies may not want to place in their existing captives. “That’s been an interesting trend that we’ve seen over the last year or so,” Ms. Brown said. Captive owners described additional ways they are expanding the role of their insurance subsidiaries. Kite Realty Group uses incident data collected through its captive insurance program to guide property maintenance and security spending, said Theresa Severson, senior vice president, insurance and risk. The real estate investment trust uses its captive to collect incident information even when they do not result in insurance claims, allowing it to identify patterns and justify investments to improve risk management, such as parking lot repairs, lighting and security. “Every dollar that flows through the captive has visibility and accountability within the organization, which changes the internal conversations that you have around risk,” Ms. Severson said. The captive also helps Kite address a specific challenge facing real estate investment trusts. Its leases generally allow insurance costs to be passed through to tenants but not deductibles, even though commercial insurers may require substantially higher retentions than those specified in the leases. By funding those retentions through its captive, Kite can recover costs through insurance premiums, she said. RSM U.S. uses investment management techniques to match its captive’s assets with potential professional liability claims that could take 20 years or longer to resolve, said Gus Springmann, director, insurance and risk financing. The accounting firm’s captive also writes medical stop-loss coverage, which provides shorter-tail risk to complement its professional liability exposures. Investment returns and accumulated surplus have enabled RSM to evaluate additional coverages, including cyber, management liability and employment practices liability, he said. United Airlines integrates its captive insurance strategy with the airline’s broader financial planning, said Andrew Nottestad, managing director — risk management. Mr. Nottestad, who reports to a senior treasury executive, said regular meetings with finance leaders give him insight into company-wide priorities, including fleet procurement and the airline’s loyalty program, and an opportunity to identify new approaches to risk financing. “That’s my chance to kind of articulate where there might be opportunities for us to think about financing risk differently,” he said. The discussions also help ensure the captive’s investment and capital management strategies align with those of the parent company. items.title: Parametric insurance fills gaps in builder’s risk coverage: panel
items.original_title: Parametric insurance fills gaps in builder’s risk coverage: panel
items.rss_title: Parametric insurance fills gaps in builder’s risk coverage: panel
items.rss_description: As the weather becomes increasingly severe and unpredictable, customizable parametric insurance can cover losses and enhance safety in ways traditional builder’s risk policies cannot, a panel of experts said Tuesday at the International Risk Management and Insurance Construction Risk Conference.
items.extracted_text: While builder’s risk covers only physical damage, parametric can compensate builders for conditions that make work impossible or unsafe, such as extreme heat or cold, wind, rain or snow, said the panel of three advisers, none representing parametric insurers. “Contractors are just absorbing (non-covered weather losses), mostly silently,” said Rose Hall, founder of construction risk advisory firm RH Business Ventures. “And most people I talk to say, ‘I’ve been working in weather for forever, and it hasn’t been a problem.’ Really?” Ms. Hall pointed to the growing impact of weather events such as polar vortexes, atmospheric rivers and heat domes. Even if it doesn’t cause direct damage, a day below 40 degrees could reduce the strength of poured concrete by 50 percent, she said. And winds over 20 miles per hour create unsafe conditions for some crane operations. Meanwhile, heat-related worker fatalities have increased. Builders face pressure to keep working under these conditions to stay on schedule, Ms. Hall said. “Weather is weird, it’s causing delays, which costs everybody money. But more than that, we’re endangering our workers by having to make the moral decision to work in hot weather or not,” said Ms. Hall, who is based in Irvine, California. Most contractors include an allowance for bad weather days in their bid, but these are typically “a rounded guess,” based on prior experience or a quick Web search on average conditions. A 10-year average can conceal huge annual volatility, Ms. Hall noted. By using more a more precise weather estimate for the jobsite location, builders can produce a “zero-weather-day bid” which embeds the expected weather delays in the budget, said Gary Kaplan, a former of president of construction for Axa XL. “That could give you an advantage” over a competitor with a weather allowance, he said. Parametric insurance is attractive because the payout can be used for any purpose, not just repairs to damage, said Mr. Kaplan, who is based in Chicago. If a freeze delayed the start or a project, for example, a payout could fund overtime once the weather improves. “The goal is not to cover every weather event,” according to Mr. Kaplan’s presentation. “It is to cover the specific events that stop your specific operations at your specific location.” Policies can be customized to a project’s operations and safety thresholds, Ms. Hall said. For example, a policy could cover cold only on days when the crew plans to pour concrete, or high winds only on days cranes will be used. Temperature trigger points can be customized to a site’s heat protocols. “This is not parametric in the usual sense,” said Chris Smith, a Newtown, Connecticut-based senior director at the Baldwin Group. “To me, this is schedule guardianship.” Mr. Smith encouraged larger builders to use parametric insurance across their portfolio. Builders with captives could use a parametric payout could fund the captive’s deductible after a catastrophic event, he said.
